By Simon Smale

Topic:FIFA World Cup

Thu 2 Jul 2026 at 6:39am

Thu 2 Jul 2026 at 6:54am

England saluted its hero, captain Harry Kane, once more. (Getty Images: FIFA/Joosep Martinson)

England needed a hero.

Trailing DR Congo by a goal and facing World Cup elimination, England needed a moment.

Harry Kane gave them two.

As England fans in Atlanta, back home in England and in bars across the world celebrated a come-from-behind victory with equal parts delight and relief, they were largely raising their glasses to one man in the midst of the most extraordinary goal-scoring season of his life.

In a week where one England captain made an arse of himself by hijacking a desperate defeat to make himself the headline, England's footballing skipper made headlines the right way, grabbing his team by the scruff of its neck and carrying them into the last 16.

The Bayern Munich man's two goals displayed all the hallmarks of the great player that the 32-year-old has proven himself to be.

The leader is turning into a legend. (Getty Images: The FA/Eddie Keogh)

His 82nd and 83rd goals for England were the fourth and fifth he has scored at this World Cup, a tournament where the biggest names are shining on the biggest stage.

And Kane deserves to be considered one of the very biggest of those names.

"If you give him a chance, it's a goal," Declan Rice told BBC Sport after the game.

"I've seen it too many times. It's ridiculous the goals he scores and how he scores them.

"His whole mentality around scoring, [that's] 72 [goals] for the season now, it's just ridiculous."

Declan Rice (right) giving Harry Kane a hug for all of England. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Kane delivered under the most extraordinary pressure of being behind in a World Cup knockout game, with the opposition keeper having a blinder of a match.

Fans were getting restless. Passes were going astray.

Tension was mounting with every passing second.

Make no mistake, England were by far the superior team in Atlanta.

Sure, the opening 20 minutes were torrid, DR Congo opening the scoring through Brian Cipenga with a superb finish that outshone some horrific defending and a poor read from Jordan Pickford in the England goal.

Thomas Tuchel said that it was "the worst start possible", and he wasn't wrong.

DR Congo had England scrambling inside the opening 10 minutes. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

But after the first TV timeout, England dominated.

"Obviously, to concede an early goal to a team that plays this style of football is never a good thing," England's assistant coach Anthony Barry noted at the break, in one of the more obvious statements uttered in the heat of the moment.

"It can normally carry you into a state of shock [but] it is something that has released our guys.

"We have taken the handbrake off. We have created many, many, many chances.

"The goalkeeper is man of the match so far. It is not a time to panic."

Panic and watching England implode tend to go hand-in-hand, but England, to their credit, never stopped pushing forward, and Tuchel never stopped believing that his system would get them over the line.

The stats say England had 16 shots, seven of them on target, forcing five sublime saves from the "incredible" Lionel Mpasi and two goal-line clearances for an xG of 2.04.

Lionel Mpasi was extraordinary. (Getty Images: Offside/Simon Stacpoole)

They also had a remarkable 40 touches inside the DR Congo penalty box, yet most of them seemed to be just beyond where they needed to be for England to score.

England should also have had a penalty when Kane was taken down in the penalty area by Mpasi.

But then again, Yoane Wissa inexplicably managed to hit the post from six yards out just moments before.

Had that gone in, England may not have recovered.

As much as Kane will take the headlines, Tuchel should also take credit for devising a system that puts his best attacking threat to the fore and for making important changes when they needed to be made to maintain the momentum that England had built up over the course of the match.

Tuchel gave the lively but error-strewn Marcus Rashford and the largely anonymous Noni Madueke as much time as he felt they deserved before making the necessary switch with an hour gone, bringing on Bukayo Saka and Anthony Gordon as like-for-like replacements.

Gordon, who hadn't covered himself in glory during his time on the pitch in the opening two matches, provided both assists.

"The substitutes came on, and put the effort in, and we won it. Well deserved, but we had to work a lot," Tuchel said post-match.

"We have to have that mindset if it is getting hard, it is getting hard, but don't lose patience and don't lose belief."

Belief? England showed bundles of it in Atlanta. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista)

Belief must be such an intangible concept for players to grasp, especially when DR Congo were delivering the sort of desperate goal-line defence that seems predestined to deny their opponents anything.

England had only once won a World Cup match after conceding the opening goal, and that came all the way back in 1966, against West Germany.

But belief and trust in England's top goalscorer is what powered the Three Lions into the next round.

Kane met Gordon's pinpoint cross for the first, his movement off the ball giving him the space he needed to nod it past Mpasi's desperate dive.

Gordon's second assist was a lovely reverse pass into the penalty area, but the finish from Kane was astonishing, a touch to turn, another to take the ball out to the right and a third to lash it at 113km/h into the roof of the net.

Not once did Kane take his eyes off the ball as he made room for himself to shoot, his instincts immaculate.

Harry Kane only looked up after the ball left his boot at over 100km/h. (Getty Images: FIFA/Joosep Martinson)

"Thomas Tuchel has based his team around Harry Kane because he is a genuine superstar," former England defender Micah Richards said on the BBC.

"It is about moments. Kane is the one who has stepped up when they needed him most. What a hero."

Former England striker Wayne Rooney agreed.

"He is such a top player. We see all the best players perform at this World Cup," Rooney told the BBC.

"He is England's superstar, and he is the hero for us."

Kane, for his part, praised the team spirit that helped England stay the course through the frustration of missed chances and the penalty appeal.

"We spoke about people having hero moments, and it can be anyone. It was me today," he said.

"We are the same as every other nation. We are through, so enjoy it. I want them to enjoy it with the fans, and then we go again in four days.

"We spoke after the Croatian game about subs making an impact, and you saw that again. Over 90 minutes, we are tough to handle. I am pleased for everyone involved, and hopefully we'll keep it going."

Harry Kane's late winner was met with joy from England's players. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

To keep the run going, England's path goes through the Azteca and co-host Mexico.

El Tri are capable of delivering a massacre at their spiritual home if England's defence continues to be ripped open in the way it has been all tournament by teams brave enough to test them.

DR Congo ripped through the fragile four like a doctor tearing off a pair of disposable gloves having delivered an enema to a static and stodgy back line — a grim picture indeed, but nothing compared to what the Mexicans could do with 80,824 rabid fans at their backs.

The Azteca does not hold happy memories for England.

It was there that Diego Maradona punched the ball past Peter Shilton in 1986, a humiliation replayed so often it's ingrained into England's sporting psyche.

England has played Mexico at the storied venue three times. They've never beaten them there.

Mexico has won 70 of the 89 competitive (non-friendly) games it has played there, being beaten just twice, the most recent being El Aztecazo in 2002, when they lost 2-1 to Costa Rica.

They are also unbeaten in 10 World Cup games there.

If ever England needed a hero, again, Harry Kane may need to get his cape back on.
